passage:
You think your Uday Chacha was always this reasonable, Ishita? Listen.
At fifteen I had one best friend, Ravi. The school cricket final fell on the same Sunday as his cousin's engagement. I wanted him there so badly it hurt. But did I say that? No. I sulked for two days, and then I said, "Fine, go. I guess I'm just not important to anyone." And later, "After I helped you with maths all year, this is what I get."
Ravi skipped the engagement. His mother didn't speak to him for a week. We lost the final anyway, and he sat in the stands looking miserable.
What was underneath? I was scared of being alone that day. That was real. If I had just said, "I'll miss you, can you come for the second half?" he could have said yes or no freely. Instead I turned my hurt into a rope and pulled.

qa.q: What event fell on the same Sunday as the cricket final?
qa.a: Ravi's cousin's engagement fell on the same Sunday as the school cricket final.

qa.q: What was young Uday really feeling underneath the sulking?
qa.a: He was scared of being alone on the day of the final; the hurt was real, but he hid it behind blame.

qa.q: At the turning point before speaking to Ravi, what could young Uday have said instead?
qa.a: He could have stated the wish plainly, like "I'll miss you, can you come for the second half?", leaving Ravi free to say yes or no.

qa.q: What was it like for Ravi after giving in?
qa.a: Ravi was caught between a friend and family; he lost a week of his mother's warmth and sat miserably through a final they lost anyway.

grounding: An uncle recalls how, at fifteen, he used his hurt and past favours to steer his best friend away from a family event instead of asking plainly.

passage:
The power went out at four, and the model volcano on Joseph's desk was still a lump of wet newspaper. The project was due at nine the next morning. Vaibhav stood in the doorway with his football boots tied round his neck.
"Trials are at five," Vaibhav said. "I told you last week."
Joseph felt the panic climb his throat. His father had already warned him about his marks. He could have said that. Instead he flopped on the bed and said, "Go, then. I'll just fail. Not like anyone cares what happens to me."
Vaibhav hesitated, looked at the boots, and slowly untied them.
They worked by torchlight until eight. The volcano stood. But Vaibhav barely spoke, and when he left, he didn't say see you tomorrow.
Joseph sat in the dark afterwards. He had got what he wanted. So why did it feel like he had taken something?

qa.q: When was the project due?
qa.a: The project was due at nine the next morning.

qa.q: Why did Joseph feel uneasy after getting the help he wanted?
qa.a: He sensed he had pushed Vaibhav into missing the trials; Vaibhav's silence and missing goodbye made Joseph feel he had taken something.

qa.q: What could Joseph have said when the panic climbed his throat?
qa.a: He could have admitted he was scared about his marks and asked for an hour of help, leaving Vaibhav free to choose the trials.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav feel about untying his boots?
qa.a: Vaibhav probably felt torn and quietly resentful, pulled by guilt rather than a free choice, which is why he barely spoke.

grounding: A boy under deadline turns real panic into "not like anyone cares what happens to me", and Vaibhav gives up football trials to help.

passage:
Monday. Lalit said he couldn't come to Sudha's house after school because he had cricket practice. Sudha sighed loudly. "Fine. I guess I'm just a bad friend nobody wants to spend time with." Lalit skipped practice and came. Sudha felt a small thrill that it had worked.
Wednesday. She wanted him to help with her science chart. He said he had a test. "After everything I did for you when you broke your arm?" He stayed till eight. His mother called twice.
Saturday. Lalit told her, in a flat voice, "I'm going to the match. Please don't do the bad-friend thing." Sudha opened her mouth to say it and stopped. She had been lonely all week, and scared he'd pick cricket over her. That was true. But she'd been using it like a rope.
"Okay," she said. "Honestly, I was lonely. Can we hang out Sunday instead?"
Lalit smiled for the first time in days. "Yes."

qa.q: What did Lalit skip on Monday to go to Sudha's house?
qa.a: He skipped cricket practice.

qa.q: What was Sudha really feeling underneath the guilt-trips?
qa.a: Sudha was lonely and scared that Lalit would pick cricket over her, and she used those feelings as a lever.

qa.q: What did Sudha do differently on Saturday?
qa.a: She stopped the guilt-trip, admitted she was lonely, and made a plain request to hang out on Sunday.

qa.q: How did Lalit feel when Sudha asked plainly?
qa.a: Lalit felt relieved and happy, smiling for the first time in days, because he wasn't being pressured.

grounding: It shows a teenager using hurt to steer a friend over several days, then stating her real feeling as a request instead of a lever.

passage:
Sharmila, you asked why your father and I didn't speak for two years when he was young. Let your Omkar Dadu tell you.
Your father was sixteen and wanted to study art. I wanted him to be an engineer. So I didn't forbid it. I did something worse. Every evening, I'd sigh at dinner. "After everything I've done for you, working double shifts, and this is how you repay me." Your Dadi would look at me. I pretended not to see.
He gave in. He filled the engineering form. And he stopped talking to me.
Two years later, I found his sketchbook under his bed. Page after page. I sat on the floor and understood that I had not asked him anything. I had only used my tiredness to push him.
I apologised. I told him plainly, "I was scared you'd struggle for money. That's all it was." He switched courses the next year.

qa.q: What did young Omkar find under his son's bed?
qa.a: His son's sketchbook.

qa.q: How did Omkar feel when he found the sketchbook?
qa.a: Omkar felt ashamed and regretful, understanding that he had used his tiredness to push his son instead of asking him.

qa.q: What turning point in the story began the repair?
qa.a: Omkar apologised and told his son plainly that he was scared he'd struggle, stating the real fear instead of using guilt.

qa.q: How might the sixteen-year-old son have felt during those dinners?
qa.a: The son probably felt trapped and guilty, giving in to the engineering form and then withdrawing into silence.

grounding: A grandfather recalls using his own hurt and sacrifice to steer his teenage son, and later stating his real fear plainly.

passage:
The school bus for the three-day science camp was leaving in thirty minutes, and it was pouring. Kamal stood by the door with his bag, rain dripping off the balcony.
Rehana, his mother, stood in the kitchen doorway. "Go, go. I'll be fine. Alone in this empty house, with the power cutting out every hour. After everything I've done for you, it's fine."
Kamal's shoulders dropped. He started to put the bag down.
Rehana saw it. She saw her own words land on him like stones. She had wanted him to stay. But she had said it as a weapon.
"Kamal, wait." She took a breath. "That wasn't fair. The truth is, I get scared alone at night since your Abba passed. I'll ask Salma Aunty to stay over. You go."
Kamal hugged her, wet shirt and all. "Call me every night?"
"Every night. Now run, or you'll miss it."

qa.q: How long before the school bus was leaving?
qa.a: It was leaving in thirty minutes.

qa.q: How did Rehana feel when she saw Kamal put the bag down?
qa.a: Rehana felt guilty and uncomfortable, seeing her words land like stones and realising she had used her hurt as a weapon.

qa.q: What did Rehana do instead of guilt-tripping?
qa.a: She named her real fear of being alone at night, made her own plan with Salma Aunty, and let Kamal go.

qa.q: How does Kamal feel when his mother speaks honestly?
qa.a: Kamal feels relieved and loving, hugging her and asking her to call every night.

grounding: It shows a parent using hurt as leverage to keep her teenage son home, then catching herself and stating her real need as a request.

passage: In the apartment lift in Kolkata, Deepika read Arnab's text again: "Can't come Saturday, it's my Dida's eightieth." Her dance recital was on Saturday. She had wanted him in the front row since Class 6. Her thumbs moved fast. "It's fine. I guess I'm just not important. After I sat through your whole football final in the rain." She hit send before she could stop. Three dots appeared, vanished, appeared. "Ok ok I'll come for the first half, I'll tell Dida I'm late." Deepika should have felt happy. Instead her stomach twisted. She pictured Arnab's grandmother cutting the cake with one chair empty. What she had really meant was, I'm nervous and I want you there. She deleted the draft she'd started and typed: "Sorry, that was unfair. Go to Dida's. Can you video-call me before I go on?"

qa.q: Why couldn't Arnab come on Saturday?
qa.a: It was his Dida's eightieth birthday.

qa.q: Why did Deepika's stomach twist when Arnab gave in?
qa.a: Deepika felt guilty, picturing his grandmother's empty chair, and saw that she had used her hurt as a lever instead of saying she was nervous.

qa.q: What did Deepika's final message get right?
qa.a: She apologised and asked for something fair, a video call, instead of using guilt to make Arnab miss his Dida's birthday.

qa.q: How might Arnab have felt reading that he was making her feel unimportant?
qa.a: Arnab likely felt torn and guilty, caught between his grandmother and his friend, which is why the dots kept appearing and vanishing.

grounding: Shows a teenager using hurt and reminders of past favours to make a friend give in, then turning it into an honest request.
